summary: Specifies how IPv6 packets are encapsulated for transmission over Fibre Channel, and how link-local and stateless autoconfigured addresses are formed on such networks. It was replaced by RFC 4338.

eli5.summary: This document says how to put IPv6 envelopes into the special boxes used by storage networks. It was replaced by RFC 4338.

questions: how are ipv6 addresses formed on fibre channel
how does ipv6 work over fibre channel
ipv6 address formation on fibre channel
subtitle: How to send IPv6 packets through storage area network cables.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel is a high-speed technology used in storage networks, but it was designed for SCSI and IPv4. IPv6 systems need a standard way to send IPv6 packets over Fibre Channel and to configure IPv6 addresses on Fibre Channel interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies IPv6 encapsulation using Fibre Channel frames with a Network Header and LLC/SNAP header. It defines how to generate IPv6 addresses automatically from Fibre Channel port names and how to map IPv6 addresses to Fibre Channel link-layer addresses.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 systems can communicate over Fibre Channel networks using the same stateless autoconfiguration and neighbor discovery as on other media. It was replaced by RFC 4338, which supersedes this specification.

today: RFC 3831 is obsoleted by RFC 4338, which updates and refines the IPv6 over Fibre Channel specification. Fibre Channel itself remains in use for storage area networks, though the deployment of IPv6 on Fibre Channel networks has been limited.

sections.title: IPv6 on Storage Networks
sections.content:
Fibre Channel (FC) is a high-speed serial technology standardized by ANSI INCITS T11, primarily used for storage area networks (SANs). It supports multiple topologies: point-to-point links, fabric-switched networks, and loop topologies. Each Fibre Channel node has one or more ports (Nx_Ports) that identify themselves with a permanent 64-bit name.

RFC 3831 defines how to transmit IPv6 packets over Fibre Channel and how to form IPv6 addresses on Fibre Channel networks. An IPv6-capable Nx_Port must support FC Class 3 (datagram service), continuously incrementing frame sequence counters, and transmission units at least 1304 octets long.
sections.eli5: Storage networks run very fast using Fibre Channel cables. IPv6 is the new version of the Internet protocol. This RFC says how to send IPv6 over storage cables.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Frame Structure
sections.content:
An IPv6 packet becomes an FC-4 Information Unit carrying a Network_Header (16 octets) and an LLC/SNAP header (8 octets) before the IPv6 packet itself. The Network_Header carries the source and destination Fibre Channel port names; the LLC/SNAP header identifies the packet as IPv6 using DSAP=0xAA, SSAP=0xAA, CTRL=0x03, OUI=0x00-00-00, and PID=0x86-DD.

Large IPv6 packets are split across multiple Fibre Channel frames in a single Sequence. Only the first frame includes the Network_Header and LLC/SNAP header. Subsequent frames carry only the remaining IPv6 data.

The Fibre Channel Header fields are set to R_CTL=0x04 (Device_Data frame), TYPE=0x05 (IP), and CS_CTL/Prio=0x0. The DF_CTL field is 0x20 for the first frame (indicating Network_Header) and 0x00 for subsequent frames.
sections.eli5: An IPv6 packet gets wrapped with address information and a label saying this is IPv6. If the packet is too big for one frame, it is split across multiple frames but only the first one carries the wrapper.

sections.title: Address Formation and Autoconfiguration
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are formed using stateless address autoconfiguration [RFC 2462]. The interface identifier is derived from the Nx_Port's N_Port_Name, converted to an EUI-64 address, then the Universal/Local bit is complemented.

The RFC specifies four methods depending on the N_Port_Name format: Format 0x1 (IEEE 48-bit), Format 0x2 (IEEE Extended), Format 0x5 (IEEE Registered), and EUI-64-mapped formats (0xC through 0xF). Link-local addresses are formed by appending the interface identifier to the prefix FE80::/64.

IPv6 addresses are mapped to Fibre Channel addresses using Neighbor Discovery [RFC 2461]. The Source/Target Link-layer Address option in Neighbor Discovery carries both the permanent N_Port_Name and the volatile 24-bit N_Port_ID.
sections.eli5: Each Fibre Channel port gets an IPv6 address automatically by mixing its permanent identifier with a standard prefix. A device learns the Fibre Channel address of an IPv6 neighbor by asking for it in a Neighbor Discovery message.

sections.title: Multicast, MTU, and Sequence Management
sections.content:
All IPv6 multicast packets are mapped to the broadcast Fibre Channel address 0xFF-FF-FF by default. The Destination N_Port_Name is set to 0x10-00-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF. Broadcast FC Sequences are transmitted differently depending on the Fibre Channel topology: point-to-point, loop, or fabric.

The default MTU for IPv6 over Fibre Channel is 65280 octets, much larger than typical Internet packets. However, the MTU MUST NOT be lower than 1280 octets, as required by IPv6. Router Advertisements can advertise a smaller MTU, and implementations SHOULD implement Path MTU Discovery.

FC Sequences MUST be non-streamed and use continuously increasing Sequence Count (SEQ_CNT) values to prevent frame aliasing. Each Exchange between two Nx_Ports has a dedicated send and receive channel. Exchange Sequence Initiative MUST NOT be transferred for IPv6 packets.
sections.eli5: IPv6 broadcast messages go to all devices on the network. The network can be very fast, so packets can be very large, but IPv6 requires a minimum of 1280 bytes. Fibre Channel uses special counters to keep track of which frame is which.

sections.title: Security and Zoning
sections.content:
IPv6 does not introduce new security concerns beyond those in Fibre Channel itself. Traditional Fibre Channel zoning based on FC Name Server masking (soft zoning) does not work with IPv6 because IPv6 does not use the FC Name Server. Instead, security must rely on Fibre Channel zoning at the frame level or on IPv6-layer security.

The FC ESP_Header can provide encryption for Fibre Channel frames carrying IPv6, and IPv6-layer security mechanisms such as IPsec Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload [RFC 2402, RFC 2406] work in a Fibre Channel environment.
sections.eli5: Fibre Channel networks have ways to block traffic between different parts of the network. Those old blocking methods do not work with IPv6, so you need to use Fibre Channel's lower-level blocking or IPv6's own security features.
